opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the problems I think about a lot, and I'd say honestly that none of the approaches we have today is sufficient on its own. It's more that each covers some of the gaps in the others.

The most straightforward approach is elicitation. If you're worried a model is sandbagging, underperforming on purpose, you try really hard to get the capability out of it. You fine-tune it on the task, use better prompting and scaffolding, give it more inference-time compute, and see whether performance jumps. If a small amount of fine-tuning suddenly unlocks a capability, that tells you it was latent all along. The nice thing about fine-tuning in particular is that it's much harder for a model to resist gradient descent than to resist a prompt. A model can choose to give a bad answer when asked, but it's much harder for it to stop the training process from pulling out the behavior. That isn't airtight, though. There are theoretical worries about models that could influence their own training, and in practice you only elicit as well as your training data and task design allow.

Then there are behavioral consistency checks. You look for weird patterns: a model that does well on easy versions and suspiciously badly on hard ones in a way that doesn't match how capabilities usually scale, or one that performs differently when it seems to think it's being evaluated versus deployed. That last one has become more of a concern as models get better at recognizing evaluation settings. If the model can tell it's in a test, behavioral evals start measuring "how does the model act when it knows it's being tested," which isn't really what you care about.

That's a big part of why interpretability is exciting to me. If you can look inside the model and see that it represents the correct answer, or that features related to deception or to "this is an evaluation" are active, that gives you a signal that doesn't depend on the model choosing to cooperate. But I'd be cautious about overclaiming. Interpretability tools are still pretty immature for this. We can find some relevant features, but we can't yet confidently say "we checked, and this model isn't hiding anything." Absence of evidence from an imperfect microscope isn't strong evidence of absence.

There's also the model-organisms approach, which I think is underrated. You deliberately train a model to sandbag or hide a capability, then test whether your detection methods catch it. That gives you ground truth, which you almost never have otherwise. The caveat is that a model you trained to deceive might look quite different from one that developed that tendency naturally, so you can't fully generalize from it.

So my overall assessment: for current models, I think a combination of strong elicitation, especially fine-tuning-based, plus consistency checks gives reasonable confidence that we're not wildly underestimating capabilities. But I don't think those methods scale gracefully to much more capable systems that might be strategically aware. That's where we need interpretability to mature, and why I think responsible scaling commitments should be designed around the possibility that evals underestimate what a model can do: building in safety margins, testing earlier and more often, and not treating a passed eval as proof of safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a hard problem, and I want to be upfront that I don't think anyone has a fully satisfying answer yet. But let me lay out how I think about it.

The thing you're worried about is sandbagging, right? The model is capable of doing X, but when you evaluate it, it performs worse than it actually could. And the reason that's scary is that so much of how we make decisions about deployment, about safety cases, about what level of precautions we need, routes through evaluations. If a model can game the evals, the whole structure gets shaky.

So the first approach, and honestly the one I'd put the most weight on right now, is fine-tuning. The intuition is that if a model has a capability but is choosing not to display it, that capability is still sitting there in the weights somewhere. And if you fine-tune on even a small number of examples of the task, you tend to recover it very quickly. Whereas if the model genuinely can't do the thing, fine-tuning on a few hundred examples isn't going to teach it from scratch. There's been some nice work showing that password-locked models, where you deliberately train a model to only show a capability given a secret trigger, can be unlocked with very little supervised fine-tuning. That's encouraging. The weakness is that a sufficiently sophisticated model might be robust to this in ways we haven't tested, and it also requires that you have good demonstrations of the task to fine-tune on, which isn't always true for the dangerous capabilities we care most about.

The second category is interpretability-based approaches. Can you look inside the model and see whether it's representing the answer internally, even when it outputs something wrong? There's some promising early work here, things like probing for whether the model knows the correct answer, or looking for features associated with deception. I'm quite excited about this direction long term, but I'd be honest that it's not ready to bear a lot of weight today. The tools are still pretty coarse, and we don't have great ground truth about what we'd be looking for in a model that was actually doing this on its own rather than one we trained to do it.

Third is more behavioral and statistical. You look for inconsistencies. Does the model do well on an easy version of the task but poorly on a hard version in ways that don't make sense? Does performance vary suspiciously depending on whether the model seems to think it's being evaluated? Does it get a question wrong in one framing and right in another? I think of this as a reasonable sanity check, but it's weak against a model that's careful. It's the kind of thing that catches sloppy sandbagging, not sophisticated sandbagging.

And then fourth, and this is maybe the least glamorous, is just making it hard for the model to tell it's being evaluated. If the model can't distinguish eval from deployment, it can't selectively underperform. That's a kind of arms race, though, and I'm somewhat pessimistic about winning it indefinitely, because the models are getting pretty good at picking up on contextual cues.

If I step back, the honest summary is that fine-tuning elicitation is the thing I'd actually rely on today, interpretability is where I'd put the research investment, and the behavioral and eval-hardening stuff is useful defense in depth but not something I'd want a safety case to rest on. And I think there's a broader point here, which is that the fact we're even having to ask this question is a reason to want multiple independent lines of evidence rather than any single clever test.

astra-6.text:
I think this is a really hard problem, because there’s an important asymmetry: if you can get a model to demonstrate a capability, you’ve shown it has that capability. If you can’t, you haven’t necessarily shown that it lacks it. It might be that your evaluation is bad, or that the model is deliberately underperforming.

One approach is to vary how you elicit the capability: try different prompts, give the model tools, or fine-tune it on examples of successful performance. Fine-tuning seems particularly useful because you’re doing more than asking the model to reveal what it can do. But you still need an argument for why that training would overcome deliberate concealment. I wouldn’t treat that as guaranteed.

Another approach is to look for inconsistencies. Does the model succeed at harder tasks while failing easier ones that require the same underlying skills? Does its performance change depending on whether it appears to be undergoing an evaluation? Those could be warning signs, although neither one by itself establishes deliberate hiding.

Interpretability could potentially give us another source of evidence, by letting us examine the computation rather than just the answers. But detecting a representation of a capability is different from reliably detecting an intention to conceal it.

So I’d want several kinds of evidence, and I’d want to test the detection methods against models that we’ve deliberately trained to hide capabilities. Even then, success on those examples wouldn’t establish that we could catch every naturally occurring case. The thing I’d be most cautious about is turning ‘we didn’t elicit this capability’ into ‘this capability definitely isn’t there.’

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between finding evidence that a model can do something and establishing that it can’t. If you get it to demonstrate a capability, that’s pretty strong evidence. If it fails your evaluation, there are lots of possible explanations: maybe it doesn’t have the capability, maybe your elicitation was poor, or maybe it’s deliberately holding back.

One approach is to vary the circumstances: change the prompts, give it tools, fine-tune it, and see whether the capability appears. You can also try to make the evaluation look like an ordinary task, so the model doesn’t know when it’s being tested. Those seem useful, but they depend on assumptions about what the model can recognise and how consistently it can conceal things.

Another approach is to look inside the model. In principle, interpretability could help us distinguish ‘it doesn’t know how’ from ‘it knows how and is choosing not to.’ But I wouldn’t assume that our current ability to inspect models is sufficient to make that distinction reliably.

So I’d want several approaches that fail in different ways, and I’d want to test them against models that we’ve deliberately trained to hide capabilities. The central difficulty is that passing those tests tells you your methods caught those particular attempts at concealment. It doesn’t establish that they’ll catch a much more capable model trying a different strategy.
